papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretability Study of an Astronomy Foundation Model
papers.source: arXiv cs.LG, accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (condensed version: oral at the NeurIPS 2026 Interpretability for Discovery workshop)
papers.tldr: A causal circuit study of the AION-1 astronomy model finds that how linearly decodable a property is says little about whether the model actually relies on it: a head that dominates probing can be ablated harmlessly, while a weakly decodable property depends on a single necessary head.
summary: Scientific foundation models are being adopted fast, but nobody knows whether their internal computations match known scientific operations. Without that, it is hard to judge reliability, spot failure modes, or learn anything new from the model.

The authors run what they describe as the first causal mechanistic interpretability study of an astronomy foundation model, AION-1, focusing on why combining galaxy images with photometry predicts redshift better than photometry alone. They localize this multimodal gain across the twelve encoder blocks and then use linear probes, head ablations and keep-only-one-head interventions to test which properties (spatial extent, dust attenuation) are used and where.

Most of the multimodal advantage sits in the first encoder block and is largest for extended and dusty galaxies. Spatial extent is causally used and one head dominates probing for it, yet ablating that head barely changes redshift predictions because the information is spread across heads and reappears one layer later. Dust attenuation is the reverse: weakly decodable everywhere, yet one head is needed for most of the gain, and keeping it alone in its block preserves nearly all of it. Takeaway: probe accuracy and causal importance can disagree in both directions, so prototype or concept analyses of a medical imaging encoder should be backed by ablation or activation-patching tests rather than probing alone. Caveat: none of the tested astrophysical operations explains what the key head computes, so the work localizes the mechanism without fully explaining it.

papers.title: MAST: Medoid-Anchored Subspace Steering for Visual Grounding in Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: MAST replaces the single global-mean steering vector with low-rank directions taken around per-task cluster medoids and routes each query to its nearest medoids; a probe-reweighted variant adds a further 8.09 points on average over MAST.
summary: Activation steering in multimodal LLMs usually adds one vector computed as the global mean of task activations. The authors argue this causes interference between tasks and unstable results because task activations form several separate clusters, and the global mean falls in the empty space between them.

MAST is training-free and input-adaptive. It groups samples by task, clusters each group into several centers, and keeps one medoid per cluster; at inference a query is routed to multiple medoids, a low-rank local steering direction is extracted for each matched cluster, and these are aggregated into the final steering vector. MAST-PR adds a small task-aware probe that reweights families of local directions.

The only number in the abstract is the average gain of +8.09 points for MAST-PR over MAST; the benchmarks, base models and margins over mean-vector steering have to be checked in the paper. Takeaway: this is direct evidence for the steering-geometry view that a single mean-difference direction can be a poor summary when activations are multi-modal, and medoid-plus-local-subspace steering is an easy baseline to try against mean steering. Caveat: no code release is mentioned and the gains are reported only for visual grounding in multimodal LLMs.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Language Model Introspection: Probing Information and Reporting
papers.tldr: The location of an injected activation perturbation is trivially linearly decodable, even in randomly initialized networks, so a model correctly reporting where it was perturbed is weak evidence of real introspective access.
summary: A popular test of LLM introspection asks whether a model can say where its activations were perturbed. If that information is already easy to read off the activations, success on the test may say little about the harder goals introspection is meant to serve, such as faithfully explaining the model's own reasoning.

The authors inject perturbations into sentences, train a simple linear probe to find the perturbed sentence from activations, and compare it with the model's own zero-shot answers across pretraining checkpoints and injection strengths, using OLMo 3 at 7B and 32B.

With an injection four times the typical activation norm at layer 0 and readout at layer 24 in OLMo 3 32B, the probe reaches 98.3% accuracy after 8.4 billion training tokens while the model's own answer stays at chance (11.1%); at the released base checkpoint the numbers are 99.1% and 89.6%. Location is decodable even in randomly initialized networks at both sizes. Takeaway: before treating a model's self-report or a probe result as evidence of internal access, check a random-init or untrained baseline, since the architecture alone can make the signal linearly available. Caveat: only one model family and one perturbation-localization task are tested.

papers.title: TabOmics: A Small, Open Tabular Foundation Model for Wide Omics Data
papers.tldr: A 7.3M-parameter tabular foundation model trained only on synthetic tables handles all features of very wide omics tables jointly and reaches a mean AUROC of 0.943 on 46 tasks, edging out TabPFN-3.5 with about 30 times fewer parameters.
summary: Omics tables have thousands to tens of thousands of features and few samples, which strains in-context tabular foundation models. Existing approaches cope by subsampling, grouping or compressing features, which can discard signal.

TabOmics is a small open family of tabular foundation models (7.3M parameters) pretrained only on synthetic tables. It processes all retained features jointly and returns predictions, attention-based feature-importance scores and test-sample embeddings from one forward pass. Evaluation covers 46 classification tasks from three high-dimensional, low-sample-size benchmarks plus synthetic feature-recovery tests.

With eight ensemble members TabOmics v2.5 has the best mean AUROC among evaluated models (0.943) and beats TabPFN-3.5 (also eight members) on 32 of 46 tasks; a single member gets 0.941 versus 0.942 for TabPFN-3.5 with eight, with no significant paired difference. Feature recovery on synthetic tables is similar to TabPFN-Wide, and predictions stay above chance at 30,000 features. Takeaway: a tiny synthetic-prior model can match much larger tabular foundation models on wide data, and its built-in attention importances are a cheap interpretability hook; code, weights and training recipes are released. Caveat: the authors note that the top breast cancer genes match the genes that define the labels, so this is concordance, not independent biological validation, and the overall margins over TabPFN are small.

papers.title: Beyond Row-Level Prediction: Evaluating and Learning Composition for Reusable Table Representations
papers.tldr: A benchmark for whole-table embeddings shows that pooled TabPFN and ConTextTab states trail simple schema fingerprints, and a self-supervised pooling objective (SCDM) over frozen ConTextTab raises the overlap-similarity correlation from 0.04 to 0.43-0.50.
summary: Retrieval, deduplication and data curation need one embedding per table, but table representation methods are mostly judged on row-level prediction, which says nothing about table-level embedding quality.

The authors build a benchmark scoring table embeddings on consistency under partial views, discriminability across label granularities, robustness to harmless perturbations, and efficiency, and compare twelve methods on synthetic and real corpora. They then freeze ConTextTab and learn only the pooling rule over its cell states with support-conditioned distribution matching (SCDM), a self-supervised loss that aligns embedding similarities with the actual overlap between table partitions.

Lightweight schema- and text-based fingerprints are among the strongest methods, and TabPFN and ConTextTab states pooled with mean, max or three other parameter-free rules fall behind them despite being strong row-level predictors. Across fifteen head configurations, the learned SCDM rule lifts Spearman correlation between similarity and partial-view overlap from 0.04 to 0.43-0.50 on synthetic data, with smaller but consistent gains on real data and in parent-table retrieval. Takeaway: a strong tabular foundation model is not automatically a good table encoder, and how cell states are pooled, plus the self-supervised objective used to learn that pooling, matters a lot. Caveat: gains on real corpora are described as smaller, and the abstract gives no numbers for them.

papers.title: What Roles Do System Prompts Really Assign? Validating and Steering Occupational Role Vectors in LLMs
papers.tldr: Occupational role vectors extracted from activations are reproducible and separable even for similar roles, yet injecting them steers behavior at best as well as a role prompt and does not stop the role fading over 30 turns.
summary: System prompts assign LLMs roles, but it is unclear what those roles look like internally or whether activation-level role directions can replace or reinforce prompting.

The authors propose a two-part validation framework for occupational role vectors on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. An interpretability check tests whether vectors are stable across runs and temperatures, separable between similar roles and consistent across in-domain and out-of-domain questions; a control check injects them during generation and measures role expression, including over 30-turn conversations. Code and data are released.

The vectors are highly reproducible and separable, but on Qwen injecting the vector alone raises role expression well above unsteered output and at best matches a role prompt; adding the vector on top of the prompt strengthens single answers but does not slow the role's decline over 30 turns. Takeaway: representational quality (stable, separable directions) does not imply steering effectiveness, so steering papers should report both, and this two-lens protocol is a reusable template. Caveat: only two 7-8B models are tested, and the authors note absolute success rates are low by design because most answers are out-of-domain.

papers.title: Data-Efficient LLM Safety Alignment Guided by Interpretable Features
papers.tldr: Using SAE activations to pick prompts that cover diverse safety features, plus adversarially generated benign prompts that trigger over-refusal, yields a 2.4K-sample alignment set (LIS) that beats datasets up to 262K samples.
summary: Safety alignment usually relies on large fine-tuning sets, which is costly and often makes models refuse harmless requests.

The authors build Less is Safer (LIS), selecting prompts whose sparse autoencoder activations cover a diverse set of interpretable safety features, then using a multi-agent adversarial pipeline to create harmless prompts that nonetheless provoke unnecessary refusals.

With only 2.4K samples, LIS outperforms TRIDENT-Core (26K), TRIDENT-Edge (19K) and WildJailbreak (262K) overall on four safety and five over-refusal benchmarks; ablations show both the safety and over-refusal parts are needed. Interestingly, filtering data with LLM-annotated SAE safety features alone did worse than their full pipeline. Takeaway: SAE feature coverage is a practical criterion for selecting small, diverse fine-tuning sets, but SAE labels on their own were not enough here. Caveat: the abstract gives no per-benchmark numbers or base models, so the size of the gains needs checking in the paper.

papers.title: When can an interpretability claim be trusted? Stability and certification of feature dimensionality, ridge leverage and the feature recovery rate
papers.tldr: Whether a feature counts as recovered by a sparse dictionary at the standard cosine threshold flipped with the training seed for 55% of features in toy models; the paper offers stable ridge-regularized metrics and recovery certificates instead.
summary: Safety arguments increasingly cite interpretability measurements, such as the share of a model's features a sparse dictionary recovers. These rely on arbitrary thresholds, so small weight changes, a new seed or a different cutoff can flip the conclusion.

Working with toy models and synthetic dictionaries where the true features are known, the authors analyze Elhage et al.'s feature dimensionality and the cosine-threshold feature recovery rate. They show exactly where feature dimensionality is discontinuous, replace it with a ridge-regularized version with proven stability bounds, and derive certificates saying when a 'feature i is recovered' claim must survive a given change to the dictionary.

The certificates held in every test and are informative for small perturbations, but certified no feature non-trivially across independently trained dictionaries, and at the standard threshold 55% of features changed recovered status with the training seed. Takeaway: SAE feature-recovery rates reported from a single seed and threshold are fragile, so report them across seeds and thresholds. Caveat: experiments are toy-only, and the authors state the proofs, code and text were drafted by AI agents under their direction.

papers.title: A Concept-Based Interpretable Framework for Clinical Text-based Prediction via Token-Concept Attention without Concept Supervision
papers.tldr: A cross-attention bottleneck between clinical-note tokens and text descriptions of medical concepts gives concept-level explanations without any concept labels, staying within 0.02 AUROC of black-box models.
summary: Concept-based explanations are attractive for clinical models, but most methods need annotated concept labels, which are expensive to get for clinical text.

Clinical notes and short text descriptions of medical concepts are embedded with a pretrained language model; a cross-attention module scores how present each concept is at each token, and pooled concept scores feed a linear outcome predictor. It is tested on chest trauma severity (private data) and in-hospital mortality on MIMIC-III.

The model stays within 0.02 AUROC of the corresponding black-box models and supports both cohort-level concept importance and patient-level contributions. Takeaway: matching inputs to text descriptions of concepts is a label-free way to get a concept bottleneck, an idea that could carry over to image prototypes paired with clinical descriptions. Caveat: one of the two tasks uses a private dataset, and the abstract does not report whether the concept explanations were checked for faithfulness.

papers.title: [Diagnostic value of prostate cancer in the PSA gray zone by the AI-assisted transperineal fusion biopsy combined with multiparametric MRI in prostate cancer within the PSA gray zone].
affiliations: Nanjing University (Taikang Xianlin Drum Tower Hospital)
papers.source: Zhonghua nan ke xue (National Journal of Andrology), in Chinese
papers.tldr: In 286 PSA gray-zone patients, AI-marked MRI-ultrasound fusion biopsy found cancer in 31.2% versus 19.0% with cognitive fusion, with the gain concentrated in PI-RADS 3 lesions.
summary: Men with PSA between 4 and 10 are hard to triage, and cognitive MRI-ultrasound fusion biopsy can miss small or equivocal lesions.

A retrospective two-center study of 286 patients with PI-RADS 3 or higher compared AI-assisted transperineal fusion biopsy (n=144), where AI marked target lesions on MRI imported into the fusion ultrasound system, against conventional cognitive fusion (n=142), each with targeted plus systematic cores.

The biopsy positive rate was 31.2% with AI assistance versus 19.0% without (P<0.05), and 23.1% versus 12.9% for PI-RADS 3 lesions (P<0.05); differences for PI-RADS 4 and 5 were not significant in small subgroups. Takeaway: AI targeting helps most in equivocal PI-RADS 3 cases, which is the setting where ultrasound-based AI would also need to prove itself. Caveat: retrospective and non-randomized, the AI works on MRI rather than the ultrasound itself, and clinically significant cancer rates are not separated in the abstract.
